prospect.name: Michael Critzer
prospect.location: Reston, Virginia, USA - currently posted there for work; previously worked in Florida and his wife appears to be based elsewhere
prospect.occupation: Construction coordinator and field engineer, currently in an office role he dislikes and describes as high profile and high stress, sitting eight to ten hours a day. Previously worked on the launch pad at NASA, climbing 352 feet of steps daily.
prospect.family_status: Married; wife described as a health-conscious cook. Father is 96 and losing mobility.
prospect.training_background: Active his whole life and played football when younger. Has always self-trained with no instruction - 'I've always done self-training. Nobody's ever really showed me what to do' - and did mostly bench and arms. Can do 20-30 pushups. Currently down to roughly 1,800-2,500 steps a day from 8,000-10,000 when working in the field. Uses an on-site gym at his accommodation but finds it too crowded to keep a rhythm going. Wants to train three, maybe four days a week.
prospect.medical: No ACL in either knee, confirmed on x-ray, from football injuries when younger. Reports tightness, occasional swelling and difficulty walking in certain weather, and says his knees are getting weaker now he is desk-bound. Separately reports losing 40 lb of muscle mass while 'doing a shot' - an injectable, most likely a weight-loss agent - during which he ate almost no protein because he was never hungry. The nature of the injection was never asked about. States he is not diabetic. Legs described as still weak.

signals: 72, and the entire motivation is holding on to function rather than gaining anything: 'My dad's 96 years old, and I'm looking at him, and I see where he's lost a lot of mobility, and I don't want to end up there. I want to be able to continue walking, hiking, whatever I choose to do.'
Already medically managed in the sense of knowing his own diagnoses - x-ray-confirmed absent ACLs, recent injectable-associated muscle loss, not diabetic
High nominal professional standing and very low willingness to spend discretionary money on this: 'not four figures, you know, not $1,000 to $8,000'
Cuts across the taxonomy in one respect: his price anchor was zero, because he understood the free content to mean there was no charge at all

objections.raw_quote: Well, I'll tell you what, if you want to charge me to do this, we can stop this right here, okay?
objections.rep_response: Did not run any scripted play. Justified the price ('Trevor's time is very valuable'), then asked what the prospect had expected, then challenged him - 'do you feel like a personal trainer would do something for free? They have to pay their groceries as well, right?' The $1,000 Primal University tier, offered to three other prospects in this same batch, was never mentioned.

objections.raw_quote: there was nothing mentioned about any money or... Transaction or a fee for his services. And none of those videos did he ever say, well, yeah, this is going to cost. So you did the hype. You got me here. Now you're telling me, oh, you're to be at least four figures.
objections.rep_response: Acknowledged the feeling ('I understand that you may be like off about it') but did not accept the point or offer any remedy, and continued questioning after the prospect had asked twice to end the call.

evidence: Explicit and repeated termination by the prospect: 'if you want to charge me to do this, we can stop this right here' and then 'Hey, we'll just stop it here. Okay. Thank you.'
Direct accusation of bad faith: 'So you did the hype. You got me here' and 'You're wasting my time now'
Stated an acceptable price well below the offer: 'There's a fee, but not four figures, you know, not $1,000 to $8,000'
No offer was ever presented and the call ended at roughly twenty minutes

Counter-evidence on qualification, not on outcome: everything before the price landed was going well - he had given a clear commitment ('let's make a commitment. If I'm going to make a commitment, let's do this') moments earlier
outcome.next_step: None. The prospect ended the call and said he would figure something else out.

notable.note: The most important marketing finding in the batch. A 72-year-old who had watched the free content, taken a setter call with Derek and booked a closer call had no idea the programme cost anything - 'none of those videos did he ever say, well, yeah, this is going to cost' - and blew up when told it was four figures, accusing the company of hype. He was explicitly attracted to Trevor because he believed he was not charging: 'For one thing, he's not trying to charge your feet like everybody else.' A $1,000 tier exists and was offered to three other prospects this same week; it was never mentioned to him. Clinically, he disclosed that he has no ACL in either knee, confirmed on x-ray, and that he lost 40 lb of muscle mass while on an injectable - and the rep's first response to the ACL disclosure was 'Do you believe that?'

quality.notes: Heavy inversion throughout, and particularly damaging in the final confrontation where both sides' lines cross labels repeatedly between 00:17:21 and 00:19:27 - 'Hey, we'll just stop it here' and 'I'm curious, Michael, I'm curious' appear under the same speaker. The prospect's height is garbled beyond recovery ('I'm 86 pounds, something like that') and his description of the injectable is fragmentary. Roles assigned from content throughout.
